entries.note: The glyph table is open-addressed with eight probes and a per-frame stamp, unlike the direct-mapped tables of the other adapters: they can re-rasterise a colliding glyph while drawing, but here every glyph must already be in the atlas before rendering starts, so two glyphs of one frame sharing a slot would otherwise thrash and one of them would never draw. Slots touched this frame are never evicted. When the atlas fills, the pre-pass resets the table and shelves and walks the list a second time so glyphs placed before the reset come back; the barrier before the copy waits for the previous frame's fragment reads, so overwriting old atlas pixels cannot corrupt a frame still in flight. Running out of copy regions or staging space keeps what was placed and leaves the rest for the next frame.

entries.note: Vertex layout, glyph placement, atlas packing, batching and blend factors copy backend_metal.m and backend_gl.c; the shaders in shaders/ui.frag are the OpenGL program line for line, so the evidence shows Vulkan pixel-identical to the other GPU adapters and therefore inside the same tolerances against the SDL reference. The only deliberate difference is in ui.vert: Vulkan's NDC is y-down, so the vertex shader emits pos.y / size.y * 2 - 1 instead of the OpenGL flip. Keep the three shaders and the glyph expressions in step: a change in one adapter changes the comparison numbers for all. SPIR-V is committed (tools/shaders.py, spec 073 decision 6) and compiled for vulkan1.3, which turns `discard` into OpDemoteToHelperInvocation; that is why open_device requires and enables shaderDemoteToHelperInvocation (mandatory in 1.3). The validation layer found both that and an HDR colour-space pick on the first run, which is what the validation gate is for.

The Vulkan adapter draws a ramp as one quad per logical pixel, each carrying the whole rectangle's shape parameters. The vertex format already interpolates colour, so a single quad with two colours would have been cheaper, but then this adapter's ramp would be the graphics card's interpolation while the SDL reference stepped it in software, and the comparison in tools/render_compare.py would be measuring the difference between two definitions of a gradient. Stepping every adapter through re_gradient_sample makes the ramp part of the contract instead. Passing the full shape rather than the strip keeps the signed-distance field rounding the ends, so a rounded track needs no special case, and a slider's track costs a couple of hundred quads, which is nothing beside a frame of text.

Two frames in flight, one command buffer each, submitted exactly once per frame. begin waits for the frame's fence only when `in_flight` says a submission owns it (a reset fence that was never submitted would deadlock), acquires the swapchain image, records texture and glyph uploads outside any rendering scope (transfers are illegal inside vkCmdBeginRendering/EndRendering, which is also why prepare_glyphs walks the list before drawing), then opens rendering. execute records draws and ends rendering. present transitions to PRESENT_SRC, submits and presents; snapshot instead copies the image to the host-visible readback buffer, submits with the fence, waits and lets present only queue the already-submitted image (the `submitted` flag guards both paths, mirroring the Metal adapter's `committed`). Vertex data lives in per-frame chains of persistently mapped 65536-vertex chunks that grow to the largest frame seen and are never reused within a frame, because recorded draws reference their ranges until the fence signals. texture_update waits for the frame whose copy last read the texture's staging buffer before overwriting it. Swapchain recreation waits for the device to idle and clears every in_flight flag.
